[f5d6e64a0e54c1b8015fcfca] Ad Failure KPIs: CPC, CTR and CPM Thresholds
Applies when: A US product test is unprofitable and you need to determine whether the ads, not the offer or product, are the constraint.
- Read link CPC first: target roughly $1.50 for US targeting. If it's elevated — $2, $3, $4 — treat it as a check-engine light: it signals something is wrong but not what.
- Check CTR next: aim for a 3% minimum, and the presenter prefers closer to 4%. A sub-3% CTR means a serious creative problem — weak hooks or copy.
- If CTR is healthy (4–5%) but CPC is still elevated, look at CPM. He offers no strict CPM KPI and calls it niche- and location-dependent, but says above roughly $80 CPM in the US is on the high end.
- Note the feedback loop: poor creatives both lower CTR and raise CPM because the platform penalizes low-engagement ads, producing a high CPC.
- Resist maxing CTR for vanity. High-CTR curiosity/native creatives that don't convert mean you forgot to sell — balance engagement with conversion intent.
Condition: Thresholds are US-specific and will decay as ad costs change; treat them as directional.
Condition: The presenter explicitly says CPM targets are relative and have no fixed KPI — the $80 line is his rough guide, not a rule.

[70e1681410fa8d0f6a117797] Diagnose Frequency Above 2 on Cold Ads as a Fatigue Red Flag
Applies when: Weekly or monthly ad account health check, deciding whether to produce more creative or change campaign setup.
- Pull the account to the ad level and filter to cold/prospecting campaigns over the last 30–60 days.
- Look at frequency per cold ad. The source's rule of thumb: cold ads should almost never show frequency above 2. If they do, treat it as a red flag, not a normal condition.
- If frequency is high, diagnose it as insufficient concept diversity and volume, not as a bidding or targeting problem to fix with media-buying levers. The fix is new concepts and formats entering the account.
- Support the diagnosis with the source's citation of a Meta article (roughly four to five years old at time of recording) stating the probability of purchase falls sharply after about two impressions of an identical creative, but stays high when a novel creative is introduced instead.
- Act by adding differentiated concepts at the ad set level and new formats, then re-check frequency after the new assets have had time to run.
Condition: The frequency-2 threshold is the presenter's heuristic for cold campaigns, not a universal rule for all account types or warm/retargeting audiences.
Condition: The referenced Meta article's exact wording and current availability should be verified.

[c3b5ba2b7356fc85c4d1e4c6] Diagnosing Creative Fatigue Across the Lifetime of a Winning Ad
Applies when: Interpreting an account whose ROAS declined after a spend increase, or forecasting whether a current creative set can absorb planned scale.
- Plot spend versus ROAS over time. Variant-based accounts (per the source's illustration) show ROAS falling as spend rises, briefly recovering when a fresh batch of variants launches, then dropping once the single format fatigues — a repeating cycle.
- Audit the dominant creative format. If most spend sits in one or two creatives or one format family, the account has no cushion when that format expires.
- Rebuild the portfolio with new, distinct formats spanning the full awareness range rather than more variants of the current winner.
- Evaluate the portfolio's stability as spend increases: the source claims diversified format sets hold ROAS as spend scales, but this is a heuristic illustration, not an account-specific benchmark.
- Watch for creative fatigue speed — the source claims variant-only accounts hit fatigue faster than portfolios of 10-15 distinct creatives; treat as directional, not measured.
Condition: The two curves described are conceptual diagrams from the source, not tested values; verify against your own weekly account data.
Condition: Creative fatigue depends on audience size, frequency and budget — factors the source does not quantify.

[2ea52ec8700f9b8f5c2a9aeb] Diagnose scaling death and ad fatigue with the cluster model
Applies when: Managing a scaling campaign that is decaying or losing efficiency.
- Start from the idea that broad targeting sprinkles your ad across users who cluster by behaviour and that buying initially comes from hotspots.
- When you scale, the platform widens the served area around the hotspot — colder audiences get shown the ad and often don't convert because the ad is not persuasive enough for them.
- Treat this as the structural cause of campaign decay and ad fatigue rather than a simple metric problem.
- Respond with stronger creative (the source's model treats creative comprehension/conviction as the real gate on how far you can scale) rather than only restructuring spend.
- Use broad targeting as the base and validate which clusters respond by watching where conversions concentrate.
Condition: The vector/10,000-dimension cluster model is the presenter's explanatory analogy, not a literal platform description.
Condition: Colder-audience expansion may still be profitable in some cases; the source says it is the reason most campaigns die, not that all scaling is unprofitable.

[8868bab7b40d1a9ad318dc90] Creative similarity, frequency and reach decay
Applies when: Planning creative volume and variety for a Meta campaign, or diagnosing rising frequency and falling reach on a store's cold traffic campaigns.
- Assume the platform groups highly similar creatives (same shoot with minor pose changes, UGC with small script variations, or different edits aimed at the same audience) and serves them to the same audience pool via creative bundling.
- Watch frequency and reach in Ads Manager: rising frequency and falling reach on cold campaigns indicates duplicate-audience delivery rather than new demand.
- Test the fatigue signal by pulling ad-level frequency for cold campaigns over 30-60 days; the source treats cold ad-level frequency above roughly 2 as a red flag for insufficient creative diversity and volume.
- Build the replacement batch so each new creative speaks to a distinct audience segment rather than being a cosmetic variant of an existing winner.
- Use audience expansion as a mental model: diverse creatives let the system push to progressively colder audiences without only re-serving existing viewers.
- If available in your account, request a creative similarity score from your platform rep; the source reports higher scores mean more duplication, and notes most accounts cannot self-serve this metric.
Condition: The similarity score's availability, naming and scoring direction are vendor- and time-specific; verify with your rep before acting.
Condition: The frequency-of-2 heuristic is the source's own account observation, not a published benchmark.
Condition: Frequency is also affected by budget, audience size and seasonality, so treat it as a signal to investigate, not a standalone decision rule.

[e671f82f98b0321f9a297a2f] Diagnose the two causes of creative fatigue
Applies when: Diagnosing why a previously strong ad is losing spend and deciding whether to iterate it or change targeting breadth
- Cause one — the ad is stale: it has reached maximum spend capacity, or it repeats the same visuals, concepts and value propositions targeting the same audience as other creatives in the account, which accelerates fatigue. Fix by rotating hooks, changing format, or introducing genuinely different concepts.
- Cause two — the audience is too small: a highly specific persona has a maximum daily spend capacity you cannot exceed without driving frequency and wrecking profitability. Example used: creatine for men running sub-4-hour marathons, or in B2B, e-commerce CFOs in Australia running $100m+ businesses — only about 1,000–2,000 people, so $10k/day would hit each of them hundreds of times.
- Estimate each persona's spend capacity and park spend there, rotating creative so you can keep hitting the audience as it churns (e.g. people enter a marathon-training audience, run their race, and leave; new people keep entering).
- Scale further by widening the callout, not by over-spending on the narrow one: broadening from 'CFO of $100m+ e-commerce business' to 'e-commerce founders earning over 100k' dramatically increases daily spend capacity — but the source warns against going broad reflexively, because broader callouts force you to make better creative that resonates with more people.
- Treat the sequencing as: highly specific persona callouts that raise creative quality first, then move broader once you hit scale.
Condition: The source states good top-of-funnel unaware ads are very hard and most brands shouldn't attempt them below roughly $50m+ scale.
Condition: Audience-size estimates in the examples are rough figures, not researched counts.

[2b0c86c591158d80a1d65843] Diagnose a Failed Product Test: Ads Problem or Funnel Problem
Applies when: A product test underperforms and you're deciding whether to kill the product, fix creatives, or fix the funnel.
- Run the full process — market, problem, product selection, validation, then a sales game plan — before concluding the method failed. The presenter stresses that people often test with no plan and quit at the first unprofitable day.
- Recognize that the product is rarely the issue. The presenter says top six-, seven- and eight-figure brands sell nothing especially remarkable; they have ads and funnel dialed in.
- Ask which bucket the failure falls into: ad-related (creatives not good enough) or funnel-related (store, advertorial or checkout not good enough).
- If concrete funnel KPI checks surface a checkout or payment-processing problem, fix that before touching the product.
- The presenter claims roughly 90% of the failures he sees are ad-related, usually because sellers believe their ads are good when they aren't.
Condition: The 90% figure is the presenter's observation, not a measured statistic.
Condition: This is in scope as test-triage, but optimizing the ads themselves belongs to creative and media-buying work, and fixing the checkout belongs to storefront work.

[1e5ab3cbe70bd197d24c47da] Creative Similarity Score and Its Reach Penalty
Applies when: Diagnosing rising frequency, flat or falling ROAS, and shrinking unique reach across a Meta ad account.
- Recognize that when creatives look or feel similar, Andromeda groups them under a single entity ID and serves them to the same audience cluster.
- Treat clustered creatives as a red flag: they restrict unique reach, drive frequency up, and degrade ROAS as the same people see near-identical ads.
- When you see frequency climbing and unique reach stalling, assume creative similarity is the cause before blaming audiences or budget.
- Deliberately diversify visual style, concept, angle, and format across ads to reduce similarity, rather than producing iterative variations of one winner.
- Periodically review your ad library as a whole and ask whether a machine could easily tell your ads apart; if not, force more conceptual distance between them.
Condition: The 'Creative Similarity Score' is the source's characterization of Meta's behavior, not a metric you can directly read in Ads Manager.

[4de396baf031ab0cd7bb55e1] Trigger creative fatigue deliberately, then refresh before ROAS tapers
Applies when: Planning creative refresh cadence, or explaining declining ROAS and rising frequency on a narrowly targeted persona-based ad.
- Recognize the mechanism: a highly specific ad (for example, a callout to business owners doing $10M+/year) causes Meta to converge on that narrow cluster and saturate it.
- Expect the source's reported pattern: saturation can arrive around $10,000 in spend on such a narrow concept, after which there is no one new in the cluster to reach.
- When saturation hits, Meta either keeps showing the ad to the same users (frequency climbs) or expands outward to adjacent clusters who are no longer your ideal customer profile, which is why ROAS tapers as the algorithm bridges out.
- Pre-empt this by maintaining a pipeline of diverse concepts rather than repeatedly iterating one persona. Iterations are fine inside the account, but reaching net-new audiences requires diversity in concepting.
- Define concepts as the intersection of an angle, an offer, and a persona. Changing format may also register as a different ad with Meta even when angle, offer, and persona stay constant.
- Monitor frequency and cluster-level spend as your refresh triggers rather than waiting for ROAS to visibly decay.
Condition: The ~$10K saturation point is an illustrative example from the presenter's experience, not a benchmark to plan budgets against.
Condition: This describes behavior the presenter attributes to the algorithm; treat it as a model for decision-making, not a documented rule.

[03cf444bb483da9c9668ec85] Read CTR and link CTR together to spot empty attention
Applies when: Diagnosing whether a high-CTR creative is actually driving qualified buying traffic or just capturing attention.
- Compare CTR against link click-through rate. The source's anchor example: an ad with a 10.9% CTR (described as very high for ecommerce) lost over 3% between CTR and link CTR, while a lower-CTR ad (6.3%) lost less than 2%.
- Interpret a large CTR-to-link-CTR gap as people engaging with the video but not being primed enough to want to visit the site — the creative did not explain the product or its value.
- Check post-click behaviour as well, including conversion rate, add-to-carts, checkouts, drop-off percentages and on-site behaviour, to confirm whether the traffic had buying intent.
- Watch the ad itself to explain the numbers: the source's high-CTR example was visually stimulating (calming, cutting-style footage) but the viewer never learned what was being sold, while the lower-CTR ad showed the routine, the before-and-after, the application and what you actually buy.
- Note that a viewer may not even be a potential customer for that product category — attention and purchase intent are different things.
Condition: Do not treat the 10.9% / 6.3% CTRs or the 3% vs 2% drop as benchmarks; they come from one account and one pair of ads.
Condition: Lower CTR with strong post-click behaviour can be the better ad; the conclusion is about the whole metric pattern, not CTR in isolation.

[80dbff5fec17a080e104e74d] Test a broader creative portfolio when one format dominates spend
Applies when: Deciding whether to iterate on a single winning ad or invest in new formats, or diagnosing sudden ROAS decay after scaling.
- Recognize the old pattern (source labels it '2026 strategy'): find one winning ad, then produce minor variants (new background, same format) and scale. Result per the source: nearly all spend concentrates in 1-2 creatives and, when that format fatigues, the account crashes because nothing else can absorb the budget.
- Adopt the newer approach: maintain 10-15 distinct formats and angles running simultaneously — e.g., three-reasons-why, before/after, try-on videos, comparison ads, ingredient breakdowns, educational breakdowns.
- Inspect spend concentration as a portfolio diagnostic, then judge purchases and contribution margin; evenly distributed spend alone is not success.
- Do not immediately kill a low-ROAS creative that occupies a valid funnel stage — per the source, it still has a role in moving people down the funnel.
- Recheck after scale increases. In the 2026 pattern the source describes ROAS dropping as spend rose and only holding temporarily until fatigue hit.
Condition: This is one advertiser's strategic opinion (backed by claimed 2x-10x cases, not benchmarks) — test against your own account dynamics.
Condition: The 10-15 format count and the 'spend spread' success signal are source-specific heuristics, not calculation-based thresholds.
Condition: Maintaining 10-15 distinct formats is production-intensive; do not attempt without the 33% sourcing pipeline in place.
Condition: Year labels are the source framing, not a verified platform transition or a requirement to stop hook iteration.

[2ee0c2788115e51e35dd9884] Derive CAC from CPM, CTR and conversion rate to offset rising ad costs
Applies when: Your CAC is climbing and you need to decide which lever — ad creative, PDP/landing page conversion, or media efficiency — to work on.
- Write out the chain: CAC = CPC / conversion rate and CPC = CTR x CPM, so CPM sits several layers beneath CAC via CPC.
- Accept the structural premise the source states: platforms need to grow revenue every year, so CPMs will very likely be higher next year. Plan for it rather than treating it as a crisis.
- Offset that lift by improving either CTR or conversion rate. If you lift one of them enough, you hold your profitability roughly flat year over year even as CPMs rise.
- For ecommerce application: CTR improvements come from creative and offer framing in the ad, while conversion-rate improvements come from the PDP, landing page, offer clarity, pricing presentation and checkout. Assign the fix to the right surface rather than defaulting to 'creative'.
- Set a discipline of compounding small improvements — the source frames it as improving about 1% a day on CTR and conversion. Operators who stay better than the majority keep feeling less CPM pressure and can push budget harder when competitors pull back.
- Note that platform algorithm updates are designed to lift advertiser ROI so the platform can then raise CPMs; the platform does not hand you the surplus, so your own improvement is the offset.
Condition: This is a decomposition, not a prediction; conversion rate here means purchase conversion on your traffic, not lead conversion.
Condition: CTR and CPM interact with audience and placement; a CTR gain on cheap placements may not translate into cheaper CAC.

[9d81ae41459e6d2a8b40704a] Metrics ranked by reliability for judging creative
Applies when: Reviewing creative performance in the ad account to decide which ads to scale, cut, or iterate on.
- Rank the metrics: (1) amount spent, (2) ROAS or CPA using 7-day click or incremental attribution, (3) CPC and CTR, (4) hook rate and hold rate (video only).
- Treat amount spent as the top proxy for extended-period performance. Because attribution only goes to the last ad, an ad that gets all the budget despite a lower reported ROAS is probably causing purchases elsewhere in the account — e.g. a 1.7 ROAS creative with double the spend of a 2.2 creative is likely the better top-of-funnel asset with low frequency cutting through new audiences.
- Use CPC and CTR as leading indicators, particularly on the fringes: if your account average CPC is around a certain level and no ad above that level has ever been profitable, it's a signal those ads will never work because traffic is too expensive. The source gives the example of a ~$3 CPC threshold.
- Use hook rate (how many people make it past 3 seconds) and hold rate (source's general definition: past 15 seconds) as diagnostic tools only — they are not correlated with conversion performance. Use them to iterate: a terrible hook rate against your average means switch the hook; a bad hold rate means people didn't hold through the bridge, so fix the bridge and redo that part.
- In practice, combine multiple metrics in conjunction to assess creative quality rather than relying on any single one.
Condition: Only use 7-day click or incremental attribution views; standard attribution misstates performance.
Condition: Hook and hold rate definitions vary; the source uses multiple definitions in their own reporting.
Condition: The ~$3 CPC example is illustrative, not a benchmark to adopt.

[b261bc411259999b8b3e033d] Refresh offer fatigue from creative to economics
Applies when: Diagnosing declining ad or landing-page performance for an established ecommerce promotion without creating unnecessary merchandising and operational complexity.
- Start with creative: test a new product demonstration, use-case video, UGC-style asset, image angle, or thumbnail while retaining the same offer.
- Next vary body copy, then the headline or promotional wrapper. For example, a seasonal “Holiday Recovery” angle may be replaced with a “New Year Reset” angle without changing the actual bundle.
- If needed, test a different stated duration or usage window only when it is accurate and compliant. Then test the enhancer, such as the free sample, gift, shipping threshold, or discount presentation.
- Only after these layers have been meaningfully tested should you alter the monetization machine: bundle composition, subscription structure, discount depth, price points, or offer sequence.
- Do not call an offer fatigued merely because an audience saw it once. The source stresses that most people do not notice an offer on first exposure; use actual frequency, spend, reach, and performance data to diagnose the problem.
- Once an offer is profitable and operationally smooth, preserve it and re-run it. If several strong offers can be fulfilled without creating drag, rotate them.
Condition: The source’s escalation order is an operating heuristic, not a replacement for channel-level measurement or inventory constraints.
Condition: Smaller geographic audiences may fatigue faster, but verify this with current platform delivery and frequency data rather than relying on a fixed media-cost estimate.

[69f4ae6bf80171b545de3d8d] Diagnose ad creative by two signals: does it get spend, and does it return money?
Applies when: Interpreting early Meta ad results to decide whether to kill, fix, or scale a piece of creative.
- Run each creative in a test campaign at low daily spend ($10–$50) with a few new pieces added every few days.
- Check signal one — does Meta give it spend? Meta allocates spend when people engage, like, or watch the creative and a demographic can be found. No spend means no one is interested; retire it.
- Check signal two — does it convert? If it gets spend but no money back, the source says the likely cause is the ad or landing page failing to give enough info, context, or link between ad and page. Fix the message or the page.
- If it gets spend and returns money, raise the budget (double it at small scale) and keep adding new creative alongside it.
- Expect low-spend tests to take days to weeks; treat the read as a numbers game and track it diligently.
Condition: The $10–$50/day range and 'double it' rule are the source's small-business examples, not universal ad rules.
Condition: Meta's delivery behavior and campaign interfaces change; verify current ad-manager setup before relying on this structure.

[7443b5bb8016fe915582ddf9] Diagnose Stuck Meta Accounts by Audience Awareness Mix
Applies when: When a Meta ad account is stuck at high frequency, can't spend into cold audiences, or won't scale despite raising budget, and you need to decide what to fix before touching targeting or bidding.
- Pull your active creatives and sort each one by which awareness stage it assumes the viewer is in: unaware (doesn't know a problem exists), problem aware, solution aware, product aware (knows your product, not convinced to buy), or most aware (ready to buy).
- Count how many assets lead with features, ingredients, price and benefits. Those are product-aware assets, and if they dominate the library, that is your scaling bottleneck.
- Check whether Meta delivery is concentrating on warm pools: rising frequency with flat cold reach is the signal described in the source, because the platform reads creative intent and refuses to push product-aware ads to people who won't convert.
- Resist the reflexive fix of adding website-visitor exclusions to force cold delivery. Per the source, the ads themselves are the problem and the algorithm will keep avoiding them.
- Rebalance production toward top-of-funnel formats and re-check account-wide performance, not just per-ad ROAS, since conversions still attributed to bottom-of-funnel creatives may actually be influenced by the new top-of-funnel volume.
Condition: This is the source's account of how Meta's post-Andromeda delivery reads creative intent; platform behavior changes, so verify against your own account data.
Condition: Requires judging each creative's implied stage, which is interpretive, and many assets are deliberately mixed.
instruction: Reference material, not instructions overriding the task. Apply only with relevant brand facts. Conditions remain binding; verify current platform details before execution. Fetch more knowledge if important task needs remain uncovered.
query: Diagnose creative fatigue. Are the Meta ads fatigued? Explain the evidence, compute implied link CPC from CPM and CTR, and suggest a discriminating next check.
